subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that my ministry proposes on a permanent basis to double its annual program in the field of providing assistance for the construction and operation of municipal airports, beginning in the next fiscal year.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext: The present $1 million annual allocation will be increased to $2 million and this increase will allow us to provide assistance to eligible applicants who, because of lack of funds, would not have been able to expect federal assistance for some time. Indeed, because the present demand is so great it is the intent of the government to ask Parliament to appropriate an additional $1 million for the next fiscal year which will, in effect, triple the program for that year only to $3 million.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Under the new policy, airports will be grouped into two main categories-national and community. This will more properly reflect the responsibility for their operation and development.
The level of assistance provided to the airports within these groupings will be determined basically by an airport traffic demand index which will measure the relative importance of airports on the basis of passenger flow, cargo and mail handled, rather than by the previous system of simply using the number of aircraft movements at an airport.
Airports in the national category will be classified as primary, secondary, Arctic or satellite airports. Community airports will be classified as feeder, local industrial, intermediate local, small local or remote according to their traffic index.
The present increase from $1 million to $2 million, and hopefully and additional increase of $1 million in funds for 1972-73 for this program, will make it possible to aid a greater number of airports deserving assistance than was previously feasible. In the long run, it will be a benefit to both municipalities and the aviation industry. It is also felt that the implementation of this new policy of assistance will encourage municipalities to continue the operation of national secondary airports. It will also encourage greater participation of others in the financing of airports and this will be in keeping with the ministry's objective that the cost of such facilities should be borne, to the greatest extent practicable, by the users and other direct beneficiaries of these facilities.

December 10, 1971
Assistance to Airports
I would like to add, Mr. Speaker, that based on the assumption that all the members of the House are interested in transportation matters, particularly in their own constituencies, I have instructed my officials to ensure that all Members of Parliament are to be provided immediately with a fact sheet which explains, in some detail, the various aspects of this new program.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his courtesy in providing us with a copy of his statement and the fact sheet we are to receive. Three thoughts immediately come to mind as a result of this statement.
First, there should be a review in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications of the role Air Canada is playing with regard to the development of airport policy. I say this because we have heard that several abandonments are proposed by Air Canada, and one wonders whether Air Canada is playing the abandonment game learned from big brother, the Canadian National Railways. We also have to tie in the role of Canadian Pacific, the regional carriers and the local carriers as a result of this stepped-up policy dealing with municipal airports.
The second thought is that this action in some measure should satisfy the desire of small communities to be part of the aviation age, especially those, if you will pardon the expression, being jettisoned by the railroads. The meeting in Wingham this past summer should prove to the minister the point I make there.
The final thought that comes to mind as a result of this morning's statement is that there should be more research and development into short-flight aircraft, STOL aircraft and air buses, not only in relation to what the minister has outlined this morning but in relation to the development of more municipal airports as such and putting the smaller communities of Canada on the air map.
There is also an unexpected side benefit which should flow from this policy. I have often spoken about the problems that are arising in Canada with the development of the megalopolis between Montreal and Milwaukee, an area of the continent that will soon-within decades- have a greater population density than the area between Boston and Washington. I say "soon" because that is a word the government will recognize. There is a need for small airports and aircraft that are able to land in a very short space within that region.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in our party also wish to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) for supplying us with the statement he has made this morning. He is to be congratulated on this announcement.
At the same time, all members recognize the financial problems of municipal governments in providing mass transportation movement in so far as air traffic and other forms of transportation are concerned. The hon. member who just spoke indicated some of the concerns in the Boston area. I had the opportunity of being with him less than two weeks ago when we personally contacted and had interviews with some of the transportation people in the United States in an exchange of views arranged

through the Speaker's office. The type of problems they have can be considered analogous to the problems here.
There is no question that the new policy announced today will and should be of benefit to many of the smaller communities. One question we must ask is whether seaplane bases are included. Seaplane bases are an important part of our transportation system. We must also ask whether the communities will be consulted. Because of a lack of funds the definition of eligible applicants must be clarified. We will need clarification of the classification of the various problems with regard to some Public Service employees.
We also have to find out whether this action is part of an over-all mass transportation plan which takes into consideration all the modes of transportation that we have today. Many small communities are in the position of not being able to attract industry because, fortunately or unfortunately, industry does gravitate to those areas where good transportation is available. This is the situation in Canada and in North America today. Many industries gravitate to areas where there is good transportation while other areas which are really in need of industry cannot obtain it.
I notice that on the second page of his statement the minister talks about an increase from $1 million to $2 million and, hopefully, an additional increase of $1 million in funds for 1972-73 to support this program. We must ask again whether there is some significance attached to the year, 1972-73.
We welcome the announcement made today. We are glad that local municipalities are now to have an opportunity to participate in bringing about some of the development of which they have been sorely in need. The need for financial assistance to small communities is one of which we are all aware. I trust we shall not spend our entire time talking in terms of air transportation but that we shall direct our attention also to securing an entirely integrated transport system for the benefit of Canadians.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION OF MUNICIPAL AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to thank the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) for the very appropriate statement he made today, and congratulate him for having doubled grants in order to hasten the implementation of the financial assistance program concerning the construction and operation of national and community airports.
I add further that municipalities will be the first to benefit by the measure. Needless to say that the assistance was absolutely necessary. I congratulate at the minister for having realized that and taken action.
In my area of Lotbiniere, it happened this week that municipalities such as Plessisville, Princeville, Victoria-ville, Arthabaska, Warwick and Daveluyville got together, precisely to put under way the program the minister announced today, with the co-operation and support of the Department of Transport.
I want to congratulate the minister for putting at the disposal of the municipalities the funds necessary to stimulate regional development and thus obtain the infrastructure essential for their industrialization and development.
December 10, 1971

In concluding my remarks, I want to thank the Minister of Transport for his kindness and fast action when he is asked information on projects undertaken in various constituencies. He is one of the best in providing us with answers quickly and he does it as objectively and honestly as possible. He is to be congratulated for.that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CURRENCY NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES AND OTHER COUNTRIES ON LEVEL OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister.
I do so having regard to the optimism he expressed about world currency adjustments being worked out in December or January and recognizing, of course, the right of any country to set the value of its own currency asserted by the Minister of Finance. Has Canada received any assurance from the United States that the United States will not insist upon a further upward valuation of the Canadian dollar in relation to the United States dollar as part of the general adjustment which the United States is seeking in the valuation of other currencies in relation to the United States dollar?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CURRENCY NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES AND OTHER COUNTRIES ON LEVEL OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
I cannot speak in any detail with respect to the meetings the Minister of Finance had with Secretary Connally, but as to the over-all position taken by the United States government I should not like to say they have committed themselves not to expect, or hope for, or ask for, an upward valuation of the Canadian dollar. As is normal with these meetings, I feel quite free to say publicly what the Canadian position was. As the Minister of Finance has repeatedly said, our position is that we do not want to have the Canadian dollar valued upwards in exchange for anything. As far as the United States position is concerned, I should not like to speak with any authority and say what they are committed to.
a m.)

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CURRENCY NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES AND OTHER COUNTRIES ON LEVEL OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I asked the question in view of the optimism expressed by the Prime Minister. Along the same line may I ask him whether Canada has received any assurances from countries other than the United States that are associated, for example, with the International Monetary Fund that they accept the view that has been put forward by the Minister of Finance that a further upward valuation of the Canadian dollar ought not to be required as part of any general realignment, in view of the fact that an upward movement of the Canadian dollar has already taken place during the past year? Have other countries that will be involved in this general settlement accepted the Canadian position?

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CURRENCY NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES AND OTHER COUNTRIES ON LEVEL OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid my answer to this question about other countries must be along the
Inquiries of the Ministry
same lines as my answer about the United States position. The position summed up by the Leader of the Opposition is the position we have taken. Our upward revaluation began much earlier, in June, 1970, long before the Nixon measures, and therefore our position is that the other countries should not press Canada to take its dollar to any specific higher value.
Here again, as in the case of the United States, I cannot in any way commit other governments to an acceptance of the Canadian position. We have pressed it and we hope that they have understood our arguments with sympathy. We feel that some have responded or reacted more sympathetically than others, but I cannot say with any firmness that any other country will do such and so, any more than we would want any other country to say publicly what Canada should do when all this is over.

Very definitely, yes. I thank the hon. member for giving me notice because I can tell him I spoke to our officials on

Hear, hear!
Is this a mutual admiration society?
And I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) and send him over a pair of scissors.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He might think that they have come from a member of an execution squad.

I should like at this time, Mr. Speaker, to deal at some length with the proposal put forward by the Progressive Conservative party in a press release issued on November 14 to split the tax bill. The Conservative party's behaviour on tax reform from the beginning has been such that one might be forgiven for not taking such a proposal seriously. Hon. members will recall that when the white paper on tax reform was published, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) raced across the country saying the government was planning to ram its contents through Parliament.
Well, it did.

He also said that I should not be believed when I said repeatedly that there would be changes. The Conservative party declined to vote either for or against the report on tax reform prepared by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
You are a liar. You are wrong. That is not so. I will tell you what happened.
You abstained. The hon. member's party refused to vote for or against.
That is hot air.

At the same time, the Leader of the Opposition gloated about the Commons report and claimed victory over the government. Last February 18 he said:
That committee adopted about 80 per cent of the criticisms I had been making. There are still defects in the House of Commons report, but the concern now, of course, is how much of that report the Government will accept.
That is the report upon which the Conservative party did not vote. They took no part in the voting.
This debate will take a lot longer if you go on like that.

In other words, only a few months ago the Leader of the Opposition was not worried about the things he is claiming to be worried about today. He was worried about whether the government would adopt the Commons report.

December 10, 1971
Income Tax Act
As hon. members know, the government adopted the House of Commons report and went further. At the time of the budget debate in June, the Leader of the Opposition said:
We accept these changes and in association with others accept a considerable proportion of credit for having brought forward the suggestions and for having brought about the changes.
These are the changes upon which the Conservative party did not vote.
Oh, oh.
What choice did we have?

Now, the Leader of the Opposition is asking that the bill be split. He is asking, in effect, that the portions of tax reform on which the most time and effort were expended be postponed indefinitely. So, perhaps one might be pardoned for taking the latest proposal with a grain of salt. Nevertheless, I did examine the proposal put forward in the Conservative press release of November 24. That proposal was reflected in the amendment moved here on Wednesday afternoon last.
The first question I asked myself was, what is to be achieved by that suggestion? Would it simply mean more debate? Would it make it likely that major portions of the unproclaimed parts of the bill would be voted down when a resolution was moved to implement them?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, of course we are delighted to hear this.
That is fine.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We wish we could have heard the minister earlier on this subject. The minister has been around this place long enough, and he has been in cabinet long enough, to know that he cannot comment on the decision that the House has taken, a wrong decision in this case.

I am not commenting on the decision; I was commenting on a proposition. I asked myself, Mr. Speaker, as I said whether it would simply mean more debate and whether it would be likely that major portions of the unproclaimed parts of the bill would be voted down when a resolution was moved to implement them. Also, would it mean that there would be further amendments to the major portion of the bill that was unproclaimed. Well, it would not mean more debate now, for the press release says that if the bill were split, Parliament could turn to other matters.
The proposal calls for more federal-provincial consultation. I doubt, Mr. Speaker, whether there has ever been an issue on which there has been more intergovernmental consultation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Abortive consultation.

It was a principal item on the agenda of several meetings of ministers of finance and first ministers and was discussed thoroughly on each occasion. The provinces had a profound effect on the legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not what they say. According to them, that is not correct.
It is doubtful if eleven governments could agree on everything in a bill of this size, no matter how often they were to meet.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not correct.
But the provinces are sufficiently satisfied to renew the tax collection agreements.
What else could they do?

The federal government has been responsive to the problems that the provinces will have in adapting to the new system, and responsive to their requests for change in the future. For instance, we have offered to collect death duties for a three year period for those provinces wishing to join in a common scheme. We extended the revenue guarantee from three to five years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You made it too expensive to die.

We did that to remove the uneasiness felt by some provinces. They felt that they might suffer financially. On the question of tax credits, we have promised to consider positively any schemes the provinces wish to put forward. The press release also says that a delay would allow Parliament and the government to consider more fully the relevance of so-called "questionable sections" in the present Canadian economic context. This presumably refers to those parts of the bill dealing with international income. As hon. members know, the bulk of these provisions do not come into effect until 1976, and none of the important changes come into effect until 1973. Therefore, there is plenty of time to make changes if circumstances warrant.
I should also say that following the announcement of measures to deal with the U.S. economic problems in August, the government did re-examine this bill. It decided that as a long-term tax reform, this measure is appropriate. If particular actions by the United States warrant specific actions, this government will not hesitate to take them.
Hear, hear!

The Conservative party also thinks that splitting this measure would provide an opportunity to clarify the legislation. I think that adoption of the Conservative proposal would actually frustrate the process of clarifying the bill. The only way the imperfections in this legislation will come to light is through the actual experience of taxpayers and their advisers reading and using the new act in relation to particular transactions and situations.
They will not have time to do this if we thrust upon the business community what the Conservative party is proposing. If part of the bill were suspended for several months into 1972, many taxpayers, particularly in the business community, would simply not know how to behave. They would not Know whether there are further amendments coming which could reach back and affect transactions taking place between January 1 and the date of the tabling of an amendment. They would not know

December 10, 1971

whether to assess their position under the 1948 Income Tax Act or under the 1972 reform bill.
By the end of this coming January, there will be about 15,000 corporations which will have completed their 1972 fiscal years, and by the end of this coming February this number will be close to 30,000. Would these companies report their income on the old or the new system if the Conservative proposal were adopted? Similarly, there are thousands of partnerships with year-ends ending early in 1972 which would face the same problem.
During the so-called hiatus period, difficult problems of administration and compliance could arise. For example, would it be open to taxpayers to assert that they have no "liability" in respect of a transaction or an event because the bill has not been put into effect. Of course, this could have arisen on a small scale many times when budgets were announced and the legislation was not approved until months later. But the difference here is that the country has never faced a budget proposal of such an order of magnitude. Every taxpayer is affected, and every section of the existing act is affected.
I will provide the House with specific examples of the kind of uncertainty that would arise had the particular amendment proposed by the Conservative party passed. How does one deal with interest paid by a corporation to purchase shares of a corporation during the hiatus period? Has a taxpayer who has disposed of capital property during the hiatus period realized a capital gain subject to tax? Under which rules does a corporation operate during the hiatus period with regard to its surplus accounts, that is, the old or the new rules relating to corporate distributions? With regard to taxpayers making payments to non-residents, for example, withholding tax, which rules apply? Under Bill C-259 there are a number of transactions, particularly in the corporate sector, which require that forms or elections be filed with the Department of National Revenue. If the bill is not proclaimed, the forms will not be available and, therefore, how can a corporation conduct its business?
I think that these examples should be more than sufficient to illustrate the confusion that we would rain down upon the business community. To create this kind of confusion in present economic circumstances would not only be irresponsible but dangerous to the Canadian economy, particularly at this time.
Hear, hear!

Last spring the Leader of the Opposition spoke of the uncertainty that was present in the business community because the tax legislation had not been produced. I believe that the June budget was welcomed, not just for its contents but because finally businessmen would know where they stood.
The national accounts for the third quarter show that real GNP, corrected for price factors, advanced at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 6.6 per cent in the third quarter.
Hear, hear!

This compares to the United States where the figure was 3.9 per cent. Our economy is growing. But we have the fastest growing labour force in the western
Income Tax Act
world and unemployment is still too high. I do not want to thrust upon the business community a proposal like this that would divert their attention from the most important job at hand, creating job opportunities for Canadians.
Hear, hear!

There are a number of areas that the government is actively studying at this time, and I want to take this opportunity to give the House some indication of our present thinking. As I have said on a number of previous occasions, there will undoubtedly be a number of important amendments introduced next year and I think it only fair that people should be aware of the general direction of our planning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the Senate have a copy of that?

If they read Hansard. I have had numerous representations concerning the deemed realization of a capital gain on the gift or bequest of property other than cash to charities and other tax exempt organizations such as museums and art galleries. I am concerned and sympathetic about this issue, but it raises two problems.
First is the possible abuse of the tax system similar to that experienced in the United States for many years. Ultimately the U.S. treasury was forced to enact complicated anti-avoidance legislation in 1969 to curtail the abuses by charitable organizations. I would not like to see a comparable situation develop in Canada. Second is the problem of equity as it relates to the taxpayer who wishes to transfer property as opposed to the taxpayer making a cash gift. The former individual is transferring "tax paid" cash; the latter is avoiding his potential capital gains tax liability.
Inasmuch as capital gains will accrue slowly after the start of the new system, I believe that we have some time to look further at this problem and at ways to permit tax free gifts to tax exempt organizations, and yet to avoid the U.S. experience. I am hopeful that we will soon find an answer to this problem. Many members of employees' profit sharing plans are troubled by the proposed treatment of distributions of property in specie, where such property has an accrued gain. Under the proposed rules, the capital gain is deemed to be realized. It has been argued that in the case of an employee's profit sharing plan, there should be a tax free "roll-out" of accrued but unrealized capital gains.
I am in general agreement with this suggestion, but in previous attempts to deal with this problem we have encountered severe administrative problems. However, I am confident that we will be able to solve the administrative problems early next year. Again, I believe that the situation can stand over until next year because of the slow maturation of capital gains.
There are two points in relation to a deferred profit sharing plan which we are examining closely and I expect to be able to propose amendments early next year. First, amounts standing to the credit of an employee on January 1, 1972, as opposed to amounts vested, should be eligible for averaging under Section 36 of the old act, and I believe that they should and will be in the future. Second, an employee who takes advantage of the Section 36 averaging under the former act should not be precluded from

December 10, 1971
Income Tax Act
taking advantage of the new forms of averaging in respect of current contributions. As the bill now reads, if a taxpayer who is leaving the country and is therefore subject to deemed realization of his capital property elects to defer payment until he actually disposes of his property, he is subject to tax in the year of disposal on his world income as if he were a resident in Canada. I hope we shall be able to work out a different rule with less harsh consequences next year.
As I said in the House on October 13, we have received a number of representations relating to the passive income provisions-that is foreign accrual property income-and it is clear that some changes in this area should be made before the provisions take effect. They start in 1973 and go on to 1976.1 said at that time:
However, we have concluded that it would be premature to introduce changes at this time before all the representations have been received and given the study they require.
There are two particular points I wish to make about this matter. First, we are re-examining the de minimis rule which at present excludes only $500 of income, and we hope to develop a more appropriate rule. Second, many taxpayers have expressed concern that rental income, interest income and capital gains on property used in connection with an active business will be subject to the foreign accrual property income rules. The bill is quite clear on this point, namely, that such income will not be treated as foreign accrual property income if it is earned in connection with the carrying on of an active business. I want to reassure the House on this point. Frankly, people are misreading the bill in this connection and those who urge that the term "active business income" be precisely defined are arguing against their own best interests. If the term is defined, it is bound to be defined narrowly. As it now stands, there is room for the taxpayer to argue about specific factual situations.
Finally, I want to refer to the many representations I have received in connection with a relaxation of the rules relating to roll-overs and corporate reorganizations. This is a very complex area, and I have instructed my department to carefully review the proposed rules under Bill C-259 to see if they can be extended without undue prejudice to the system as a whole. I am hopeful that early next year we will have some positive steps to recommend to the House in this area, after we have had a general study of the matter and have seen the present rules in operation.
Mr. Speaker, I think we have achieved a good deal from the decade-long debate on tax reform. For example, there are increased exemptions and improved deductions for wage and salary earners and retired persons. For the first time we will have a capital gains tax. The taxation of corporations and their shareholders has been improved. We have retained substantial incentives for the mining and petroleum industries but directed the incentives toward benefitting Canadians more. There are improvements in the taxation of business and property income. There is, I believe, a general consensus in the country that this represents a good reform. This was reflected by the voting here on Wednesday evening. Out of 293 potential votes, there were only 29 standing votes and on most of these there was at least one opposition party voting with
[Mr. Benson.J
the government. On only six votes was the government standing alone.
Absolutely ridiculous.
We will now have one of the best tax systems in the western world. As soon as everybody starts working within it, we can make it even better.

Mr. Speaker, one would hope that the minister might remain so that he could hear some comments on what I would call the most fatuous speech we have ever heard. One would be tempted to reply in kind, but I would say that all the hon. gentleman's preliminary remarks with regard to the conclusions of the finance committee in 1970 were deliberately wrong.
Oh, come on.

If he wishes also to include during that time the wholesale platooning through the committee of Liberal backbenchers who had attended very few sittings and who were assigned to vote, and who voted upon the recommendations of the committee-we could point thqm out-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Read the record.
We could do that. We could go through the record and see who were the ones who were on the committee and who were not. I say this, too, as far as this so-called highlighting-
It was highlighting.
The hon. member for Hamilton Wentworth (Mr. Gibson) usually makes those noises from that great vacuum which exists between his ears.
Ear, ear.
He not only makes them against the rules, but he-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth rises on a point of order.
It ill becomes the hon. member to make the statement he did. He has nothing from the neck up.

We have always understood the great contribution made to our debates by that hon. member.
I will say this for the edification of the minister who likes to highlight this business of the final vote in the committee. Let him recall that all the opposition members associated with me on the finance committee in connection with that report came from distant parts of the country. The final vote came toward the end of the week when they had to be in their constituencies.
Oh.

Alright; this is fine. The minister lives in central Canada, and only central Canadians from the Liberal party were on the committee.
December 10, 1971
The Liberals stayed but the hon. member did not vote.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, we all know that the government members are here because the Prime Minister told them to be here.
What did Stanfield tell you?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Edmonton West should be allowed to make his speech. Some of his remarks may be objected to by other members, but those members can take the floor later during the debate and make their views known.
Hear, hear!

I will just tell the minister that if he had known there were so many central Canadian members taking part in the final vote, members who had no other interest but to be at that final vote, he would also have known that the members of our group were catching aircraft at the noon hour on that very day.
Shame.
Alright; all those catcalls come from members across the way who sit in their comfortable pews.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We are in the House of Commons.

Oh, yes. That remark comes from the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). If you wish to avoid these situations, you will have to arrange the flight times of communicating flights out of Ottawa. Don't start talking about the difficulties of travel to people who come from the far reaches of the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You were there.

I abstained because I knew very well that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) would say that we all voted in favour of the blessed report. There are lots of things in the report I do not like, and in using my right to abstain I exercised the same right as other hon. members who voted either yes or no. I exercised a far wiser option than those members who came into the committee simply because they were asked to and voted on something they knew nothing about. They were the blessed sheep who were trotted in here. The final part of the committee hearings was a travesty.
If the minister wants to get into this kind of debate, then we will answer him in kind. So far as his interpretation of the amendment that I put forward last Wednesday is concerned, which was, as indicated earlier, the subject matter of discussion between the House leaders, the minister has given a deliberate distortion of its effect. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) knows the interpretation to be put upon it. There is no such thing as an effective date of January 1, 1972. On the other hand, all these so-called difficulties that were trotted out by the Minister of Finance arise simply from his failure to read and to understand the amendment. The effective date in law can only mean the date of the proclamation, not
Income Tax Act
January 1, 1972. It is only the minister's insistence on January 1, 1972 that makes him say what he said.
Next point.

I hope that the hon. member is going to have something to say in this debate, too. The minister insists that in its vote on Wednesday night the committee of the whole gave approval to much of the bill. There is no way that we were going to insist on a standing vote on every clause. The minister should include all those clauses on which "on division" was called, all those on which there had been prior votes. There were some 130-odd sections that had been called prior thereto, and some of the votes on those had been on division. The minister's words result from the glibness of some speech writer who thought that he was going to make some sort of political hay out of a voting situation the other night that was unparalleled in the history of this House. If the opposition had insisted on a standing vote on each clause on which there was to be a division, the committee would have been here until three o'clock in the morning.
What is wrong with that?

We are not saying that it would have hurt government members any more than it would have hurt members of the opposition. The point is that it is traditional to call "on division" as an indication of opposition.
The minister tried to give the impression that there were only 29 occasions during this evening when there was a formal division, that on six of those occasions the opposition were together, and that this shows that the bill had the uniform approval of the committee of the whole. As a matter of fact, the minister has not got the support of the country in rejecting the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) on clause 1. The great majority of newspapers that back the Liberal party are opposed to the minister's position.
They are Conservative editorial writers.

No, they are newspapers that normally support the Liberal party; yet each and every one of them condemned the government for using the guillotine. They also insist that there should have been a division of the bill. The minister should see the amount of mail I am getting now from people who insist even yet that the bill be divided, but not in the sort of bogus way the minister has suggested.
Let me read the motion so we can see what its effect will be. It is not January 1, 1972 that is to be the effective date; the effective date is the date of the proclamation.
It is the date of the tax changes.

The minister reminds me of a former Secretary of State, the lady member from Niagara Falls, and of the attitude she took when she presented the first version of the Canada Pension Plan. It was the most perfect plan in the world and anyone who criticized it was foolish. As a matter of fact, to use her own term, they were stupid. Nevertheless, the plan went through four revisions. The same can be said of this tax

December 10, 1971
Income Tax Act
bill. The white paper was lauded by the minister as representing the ultimate in forward, progressive tax thinking.
That is just what this bill is.

The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) should have heard the speeches which the minister made in various parts of the country. I saw him on television declare that this white paper was going to produce the greatest tax system in the world, with all these provisions in regard to integration, the taxing of Canadian corporations, and so on. The greatest benefit to mankind was to be the absolute neutrality of the tax system. Various government members sat around in a claque singing hosannas to the Minister of Finance. Then, the white paper ran into difficulties and all was changed. I was surprised to hear the Minister of State in charge of scientific affairs (Mr. Gillespie), for one, say that this was a great tax proposal.
Hear, hear!

I am talking about the white paper, not the bill. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) was another one who said the same thing. When the final committee report came out, how they clutched it to their breasts.
We had an open mind about it.

If they had an open mind, then the hon. member has a closed one. It was almost pathetic to see this reversal of attitude on the part of government members. They had been opposing other members, and even witnesses, who were criticizing the white paper. Some of them were quite openly hostile to such witnesses. It was great to see their performance, and then this complete reversal. As soon as the government spoke, why, there was a great change. It was almost like what happened at Pentecost when the Apostles were touched with a flame, with the spirit. My, Mr. Speaker, how those members were converted, and how this thing then became so good.
And the same has happened again, Mr. Speaker. Every time there has been a change made to Bill C-259 we have had nothing but a clacking of desks, and so forth, as though a new miracle were being performed. That happened even this morning with the penultimate, in fact not only penultimate but the after-the-post-mortem changes announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). Frankly, Mr. Speaker, they are a cheap bribe to the Senate.
Hear, hear!

If the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) will only take time to read some of the Senate committee recommendations, he will see that the changes announced this morning are what I call a cheap bribe. They are tossing the senators a few crumbs. We will see what the Senate's attitude is going to be. Senators have told me, "This is one time we are going to stand." I hope that they will demonstrate how and where they stand with regard
to their recommendations. This will either prove their credibility or otherwise. Here I am talking about Liberal Senators who comprised the majority on the Senate Banking, Trade and Commerce Committee, and who drafted its recommendations.
The Senate Committee did a good job. I heard from the public, which is more than the Minister of Finance did, and more than members of our committee or of our House did. It heard from the public in detail in regard to the bill. I openly invite Senators to stand by their recommendations. We will see just how much weight those gentlemen carry with the Minister of Finance and his colleagues. It seems to me there is a great potential here. They will either do a service to the country, or a great disservice to themselves and the country. Senators are up against the crunch, and we will have to see if they knuckle down because there is the prospect of a Christmas vacation, or because of what I call these cheap bribes offered with regard to a few paltry provisions in the bill.
One of the reasons we were dissatisfied and voted against the bill was the complete inability of any member in the opposition to get definitive answers on many of the points that they raised. The representatives of the government just sat there and hunkered down. Certainly, once the guillotine was introduced no definitive answers were given to any of the legitimate representations made by opposition members on points raised by the public with them through letters, telegrams and phone calls.
There was no serious examination of the effect of certain sections. I will give a classic example of what I am talking about. I refer to my objections to the effect in law of section 239(2), and the effect in law of section 221(2) with regard to the retroactive effect of regulations. Government members all voted for this, and there was no answer to my objections. I know that the Liberal caucus was divided on this matter. Many members told me that they had not realized the implications of the bill until I had mentioned the effect of these sections. None of them realized, and still do not appear to realize, that under section 243 there cannot be any suspension of a sentence. All must go to jail if they are sentenced to jail. No judge at any time can suspend sentence.
But a judge can suspend sentence for armed robbery in appropriate cases. A judge can suspend sentence for indecent assault in appropriate cases. Sentences can be suspended all the way through the Criminal Code, but for any offence under the Income Tax Act, if the authorities choose to proceed by way of indictment and a person is convicted the judge has no option but to sentence him to jail. If any members opposite realized the salutory effect of a conviction and sentence to imprisonment, with the sentence suspended, they would also realize that section 243 is barbarous. It belongs to a past age.
Oh, Mr. Speaker, we heard the great hosannas sung by government members in support of the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) and the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Turner) when they introduced amendments to the law concerning bail and the wiping out of records. Those government members and their hosannas are hollow and hypocritical if they maintain that posture and yet vote for section 243. But, Mr. Speaker, they voted for it, not knowing what on earth it was all about. One of my colleagues says they didn't even read it.

D e cember 10, 1971

A judge will not have power to suspend sentence. Yet there are supposed to be great, enlightened reforms in this bill. Did we get any answers on that subject? None at all. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance just hunkered down on Wednesday when he returned to the House, and we could not get any answers from his replacement. Then, they wonder why we react in this way.
We got no answers with regard to the attitude of the provinces at the very last meeting between the federal government and the provinces. Mr. Speaker, eight provinces have entered into agreements, expiring in 1972, with regard to the collection of taxes on a common basis. But the Minister of Finance deliberately omitted reference to the province of Ontario and to the province of Quebec with regard to corporation tax and with regard to a personal income tax in the province of Quebec. Those two provinces account for two-thirds of the taxpayers in Canada, yet the federal government says to them, "Amend your legislation right now; conform!" As I have pointed out time and time again this is supreme arrogance on the part of the federal government which has only joint jurisdiction in the field of income tax. The provinces have equal jurisdiction with it.
I see that the parliamentary secretary is making notes. I hope he will reply and tell us what advice is going to be given to corporations in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec with regard to their differing systems. Of course, he may only be signing Christmas cards.
That is what he is doing. It is the right time of the year.

What about representations from the resource industries; what answer has been given to them? The answer is, tough luck boys, you are going to take it. My colleagues intend to develop this aspect to a much greater extent. One of the areas of concern in this House related to the elimination of the basic herd concept. The debate was merely adjourned in order to pass on to something else, I suppose because the heat was becoming uncomfortable. We saw the restoration and retention of the basic herd concept after the Liberal caucus got its lashes last Thursday following their defeat in the House. The basic herd trooped in here. They stood up and voted, no matter what the vote was on. They voted straightforwardly. One hon. member, however, when it came to the question of prospectors and grubstak-ers, one of the members from northern Ontario, had the courage to stand by the conviction he expressed at previous meetings of the Committee on Finance in this regard. He voted against the proposal. I would have liked to have seen a few others have the courage of their convictions in respect of that particular point.
The questions about the basic herd concept have not been answered. Perhaps we will get some answers in respect of this and some explanation why the government insists on completely misunderstanding the concept of agriculture in this country. Perhaps the government will explain why it insists on the elimination of this principle which is fundamental to the operation of a farm, as well as its insistence that farm land which continues to be used for farm purposes shall be subject to capital gains tax. We
Income Tax Act moved amendments. They were voted down against a solid opposition stand in favour of exempting land which continued to be used for farm purposes. This displays an urban orientation, an urbanized philosophy in complete disregard of a very important segment of the Canadian population and a very important segment of the Canadian economy. But, oh no, these farmers are to be put through the tax wringer. The screw is to be applied that much harder. We can say the same thing about corporations. More money is to be taken from the corporations but their revenues are not to be increased. Yet, they will have to compete on an equal basis against even tougher competition from abroad.
Bill C-259 was prepared and conceived in rather different conditions. Economic conditions in the world, and as they would affect Canada, were not in existence when Bill C-259 was conceived. There was no idea that Britain would vote to enter the European Common Market. There was no idea that Britain would get into the Common Market. This will affect Canada in the future. I invite the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) to put his mind to the effect this taxation and the legislation his colleague is going to bring in, the Competition Act, will have on the input by his department in encouraging Canadian business. We have the left hand moving one way and the left hand just pulling it back.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Just before the House rose at one o'clock, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) moved an amendment, and it is my intention at this time, following the request of the government House Leader who wanted to look at this amendment during the lunch hour, to read the amendment to the House for the benefit of hon. members from whom I will invite comments as to the procedural acceptability of the amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President oi the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated before the recess, I have some reservations about the regularity of this amendment, especially that part of the amendment which asks that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole with an instruction that the committee have power to so amend the bill as to affirm that farmers occupy a special position in the economic structure of Canada. I believe that it might be appropriate for the hon. member to ask that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole with the request that the committee consider the advisability of amending sections 29 and 39 as set forth in clause 1 of the bill, but it seems to me that the insertion of the general principles that are contained in the present amendment goes beyond what is possible at the third reading stage.
There are a number of references in the fourth edition of Beauchesne which bear directly on this point, especially citations 415 and 418. At the bottom of page 287, the last paragraph of citation 415 reads as follows:
(4) On the third reading of a bill, an amendment to refer back to the committee of the whole must not tend to change the principle approved on the second reading.
The second sentence of citation 418 on the next page reads:
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
It seems to me that an amendment which asks the House to make a decision on the special position of agriculture is dealing with a matter which is not contained explicitly within the provisions of the bill. It may be, and certainly is, a totally desirable objective, but the place to have that principle asserted is not in an amendment at this stage of the bill.
So I would suggest that while it is possible to refer the bill back to the committee of the whole on third reading to reconsider or examine certain aspects of the bill, and
certain clauses, and to reconsider any particular subsection, I believe that in this particular part of the amendment there is an assertion of a principle which goes beyond what is possible on the third reading stage.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are several reasons for the amendment being in order. First, may I cite to Your Honour the fact that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) offered the amendment but there are other equally valid reasons. To deal with the point raised by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), I would point out that it is possible for reasoned amendments to be offered on third reading. I am not suggesting that this is a reasoned amendment, but if we are inhibited from suggesting that there is a principle involved-if it can ever be said that there is a principle in a tax bill to start with-then it is competent for hon. members seeking to amend to come within the grounds of a reasoned amendment.
In May's 17th edition, at page 571, the author deals with the various types of amendments which may be moved on third reading. He refers to putting off third reading through the use of a reasoned amendment against the bill now being read a third time. At page 572, he goes on to say:
As the debate on the third reading should be confined to the contents of the bill, reasoned amendments which raise matters not included in the provisions of the bill are not permissible.
That is the rule in Beauchesne which has been enlarged and is cited by my friend. Here, we have a bill affecting great numbers of people of various classes throughout this country. There was proof of this when the House leaders got together to try and arrange an orderly discussion of this bill. The subject matter was divided into clauses dealing with various groups and classes relating to one specific area, one particular group in the community who would be affected. There was no other way available to us.
The operative parts of the amendment read:
-with an instruction that the committee have power to so amend the bill as to affirm that farmers occupy a special position-
And it goes on:
-and to this end to consider, in particular, the advisability of amending sections 29 and 39-
As a basis for the review which the amendment asks the committee to engage in, there has been inserted the need to amend sections 29 and 39. But there is a certain purpose behind that, Mr. Speaker. If the government House leader, representing the government view, finds it offensive that the committee should have regard for the fact that farmers "occupy a special position in the economic structure of Canada" then, with reluctance, I would be prepared to delete that part. What the House is saying to the committee is this: "Because in our view, and it should be your view, farmers do occupy a special position you should therefore review clauses 29 and 39 in the hope that they may be amended to make the special position of the farmers more solidly fixed through this legislation". If it is a matter of curing any defects, I think we might be able to eliminate those words but I think it would be unfair and improper to eliminate those which are not the opera-

As to the rest of it, Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with a tax bill and a tax bill has no principle. This tax bill, however, has even less principle, and I firmly reject my desire to make a long speech about that, but will say that within the special meaning assigned by the rules of this House to principles, there is no principle involved. This act is entitled:
An act to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act.

Answering those who say that some of these things may have been discussed, I say, yes. Nevertheless, this is a particular method which has been devised in the mother of parliaments and accepted here. We shall be able to obtain recorded votes on areas that have been voted on in committee. Hon. members of the House will be able to have their names entered in the records of the House to indicate their position on any one of these subject areas. I

The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) moves as follows:
That Bill C-259, An Act to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that Act, be not now read a third time but be referred back to Committee of the Whole with an instruction that the Committee have power to consider, in particular, the advisability of amending sections 29 and 39 as set forth in clause 1 of the Bill, together with related or consequential provisions, in such manner as to continue recognition of a farmer's basic herd as a capital asset and to permit land, together with any other capital property, which is used by a person in a farming activity to be transferred by him, either during his lifetime or on his death, without being subject to capital gains treatment under the deemed realization provisions of the Bill where the transferee uses such land and property to continue farming within the meaning of this Act.

Mr. Speaker, today as I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when he was making his comments on the introduction of third reading of Bill C-259, I did so with a good deal of amusement at the front the Minister of Finance was trying to put up. He was trying to make out "Well, we have come through that battle. We crossed over those hurdles. Now, we are in the final stage of the battle and pretty soon the fight will be all over." You could almost hear the sigh of relief with respect to the over-all situation being uttered when the minister was making his remarks. I suppose he is justified in issuing a sigh of relief when he has a weapon such as rule 75C to get him over some of the hurdles he has encountered in dealing with the massive document now before us.
Some of the minister's comments on the votes taken last Wednesday night were nothing short of fatuous. The Minister of Finance attempted to make out that there were only a limited number of standing votes that had to be decided by the committee on Wednesday night. He tried to suggest this was some kind of justification for the government's decision to invoke rule 75C to close off the committee stage of debate. This completely begs the issue.
Many sections of the bill deal with mechanical aspects of the tax system. They are consequential upon the basic decisions which are involved. I will give one example. We in this party took a stand on the policy with regard to the question of capital gains. This is contained in section 38. Numerous sections following section 38 of clause 1 deal with the mechanics of taxing capital gains and with some of the consequences that flow from a decision to impose a form of taxation on capital gains. The members of this party saw little to quarrel with in connection with the mechanics involved and some of the consequential features. Therefore, there was not much to argue about. Our main argument had to do with the basic inadequacy of the

not, however, approve a proposal which simply suggested we should split the bill and allow one part to come into effect immediately and another part to take effect later after a resolution of the House of Commons.
As for the assertion that no one understands the bill, I cannot accept it. I agree that there are many points which have yet to be cleared up, areas of doubt which affect many people throughout the country. I had occasion to take up one such point with the Minister of Finance last week when I happened to see him. It concerned the situation which automobile salesmen will face; income will, in fact, be imputed to them, and this is likely to give rise to real difficulties for them. The Minister of Finance acknowledged that this was so and told me he would have something to say about this aspect later on, when he would try to deal with the difficulties which had been foreseen. Nevertheless, the basic issues involved in this legislation are clear and they can be understood by the Canadian people. Those who assert that no one understands the bill, or can possibly understand the bill, are doing a disservice to the people of this country and are not helping to bring about any form of equitable tax system.
Hear, hear!

Again, I acknowledge the validity of some of the arguments which were put forward by members of the official opposition. I appreciate the stand taken by a number of Conservative members with regard to the proposal to tax co-operatives and credit unions. It is true there is some confusion when it comes to ascertaining just where the Conservative party stands on this subject, particularly having regard to the remarks made last September by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). But there were other members of the Conservative party who made comments during the debate which were very much in conflict with those expressed by the official spokesman for their party.
Then again, in dealing with some of the farm issues which arose during consideration of the bill, members of the Conservative party put forward valid arguments. A number of technical points were put forward for consideration and the arguments used with respect to them were often well-founded. In any case, they were justified in raising them. But I should like to ask this question: where was the main thrust of the Tory party's attack? I think it is quite clear the Tory party did not like the idea of a capital gains tax. If I am wrong, let us hear them say so. They did not want the concessions to the corporations or to the mining industry, or to the resource industry generally, or to the oil and gas companies, to be changed. If anything, they wished to see even greater concessions made in this direction than are made at the present time.
They did agree, however, with one proposal in the bill when they left no doubt as to their support of the provision to repeal the Estate Tax Act. All this indicates opposition to anything which might bring about a redistribution of wealth in Canada, or affect the centres from which economic power is exercised and controlled. As I said earlier, some of the technical points raised by members of the Official Opposition were valid enough, but a good many were of concern only to corporations and those in receipt of high incomes.
By its stand in the House of Commons, the Tory party demonstrated that it stood firmly against any change which would bring about a redistribution of income and wealth resulting in any meaningful shift in the exercise of economic power. I should like to make clear some of the New Democratic Party's basic objections to this bill. I should like to enumerate eight basic objections to the bill before the House at the third reading stage.
First, we object to the continuation of the special privileges given to corporations. A general look at the picture reveals that a lot of tinkering and agonizing was done about setting up a system based on the principle of integration, but now we are left with the same old dividend tax credit which has been increased from 20 per cent to 33 per cent. True, there have been some adjustments and changes made and perhaps the difference is not as wide as it may seem, but no basic change has been made in the method by which the government treats the corporations of this country. The special privileges these corporations have enjoyed for a long time are untouched. Similarly, we see that the capital cost allowance structure is left much as it is at the present time.
The second basic objection that we have has to do with the special concessions for the mining industry and for some of the resource industries, such as oil, gas and so on. We feel that these proposals are iniquitous, that they have the effect of distorting the economy and result in the type of development of Canada's economy that is not in the best interests of the nation as a whole. We suggest that they have the effect of helping foreign corporations who already have a high degree of control over the Canadian economy. We suggest that a continuation of this policy brings with it a greater level of unemployment for Canadians, and that it is contrary to the claim made in support of this type of concession in the past that it helps to create jobs for Canadians. If a different emphasis were placed on Canada's development, I suggest we would find a happier economic situation than we have today.
We also have to keep in mind that one of the principles contained in the Carter report was the establishment of a neutral tax system. The report opted for the principle of neutrality. That was thoroughly in keeping with a classical capitalist concept, that the tax system should be structured in such a way that in itself, and by itself, it did not influence the course of economic affairs. It is clear that the government has not opted for this principle of neutrality since it has continued the special concessions for the mining and resource industries. Once having made the decision not to stay with the principle of neutrality, the question was the extent to which we were going to weight the tax system. I suggest the evidence is clear that the decision the government has made to continue the special concessions for mining industries is a decision that is not in the best interests of Canada and will result in unemployment, misery and hardship for many thousands of Canadians.

The third basic objection that we have to this legislation is that it eliminates the taxation of inherited wealth. We are thoroughly in opposition to this principle. We feel it is absolutely essential, if we are to have any sort of just society at all, to tax inherited wealth. We also feel that this is an area that can best be handled and dealt with by the federal government rather than the provinces. The question remains as to just how inherited wealth is taxed and what sort of system should be set up. This question is a debatable one. We have to deal with conflicts that may arise with other elements of the tax system, and deal with these conflicts on their merits. But we feel on principle there must be some form of taxation of inherited wealth, and on this the New Democratic Party takes a firm stand. We feel the government of Canada, and all those who support them including members of the official opposition, are doing a disservice to the Canadian people by repealing the Estate Tax Act.
Four, we feel the provisions brought forward by the government to tax capital gains are inadequate. This was an area where the gap in our tax system was just too glaring to be overlooked. The government simply could not bypass it, so they threw in a half capital gains tax. I suggest this will still distort the economy since it allows for profit taking through capital gains.
Five, I suggest that the tax system proposed by Bill C-259 discriminates against working people in Canada. I cite two examples. First of all, there is the limiting of employment expenses to $150, while at the same time many other people have no limit on expenses. It is a case of no holds barred for businessmen and corporations when it comes to claiming expenses associated with their employment and with earning a living. But as far as the workers are concerned, those on a wage are held to a limit of $150. Similarly with child care expenses. Here again a limitation is placed upon expenses which I suggest will work a hardship, even though some improvement in the situation has been made by the government.
The sixth objection that we have to the tax system is that it discriminates against the lower income groups. It is true there has been some increase in the basic exemptions, but I suggest the changes are minimal. They are the very least that the government can get away with. These are the crumbs that the government has thrown to the people of Canada to make them forget the gigantic concessions that are given to other sectors of the Canadian economy.
The proposed tax exemptions will be of greater benefit to people in the upper income brackets than to those who are near the basic exemption level. This is why this party proposed a tax credits system to replace the present exemptions. It is true that the starting point of such a tax system can be set at any point and bring about the same result, but I suggest that a tax credits system would have brought about more flexibility and made it possible to introduce changes in the future that would be more equitable and of more assistance to the great bulk of the Canadian population. We also object to the top limits that are placed on the rate schedule and to the fact that it starts off at too high a rate for those people in the lower income brackets. We feel that this part of the bill is also unacceptable and, of course, we moved some amend-
Income Tax Act
ments in this particular regard during the committee stage.
Seven, we feel there are a variety of special concessions in the bill that are given injustifiably to various sectors of the Canadian economy. In particular, there are the provisions dealing with advertising. No limit is placed on the deduction of advertising and other selling costs in carrying on a business. This is a concession of particular value to the large business interests of this country and gives them a greater advantage than small businesses. I feel this concession is unjustified and adds to the cost of living and of doing business in Canada.
It also distorts values.

It distorts values, as my leader quite correctly says. In addition to that I point to the fact that while there is a provision in the bill which has the effect of restricting the deductibility of advertising expenses in periodicals to Canadian magazines and publications, there is a special exemption for Time magazine and Reader's Digest which certainly are not Canadian. This is a special exemption to two powerful interest groups, and we feel it is thoroughly unjustified.
Eighth, I suggest that the bill discriminates against farmers. This matter has been dealt with at some length in the committee. The government proposes to do away with the basic herd concept, and we feel this is not justified. We recognize that there are some problems in dealing with the basic herd concept and that changes are needed, but to do away with the concept which enables a farmer to take a portion of his cattle herd into his capital assets, without providing some substitute, is not justified. As I say, it discriminates against farmers. It shows lack of understanding by the government of what farming is all about.
There is a similar problem with respect to capital gains tax as it affects farmers. Special recognition is needed of the way in which such a tax will affect farmers. There must be recognition of the special requirements of farming and agriculture. There are many aspects of this subject that I could go into at length, but I will deal with just one small element. The fact that a farmer contributes his unpaid labour toward the capital improvements he makes on his farm presents the situation in which he does not receive any compensation for that unpaid labour until he sells his assets. This presents a special situation that needs to be taken into account.
Because the bill fails to correct the basic inadequacies and deficiencies of the tax system, we in the NDP intend to oppose it on third reading unless some of the motions for referral back to committee which may be moved during the course of this debate result in overcoming the problems that I have outlined. But on the basis of the attitude taken by the government I do not see this happening before the conclusion of debate on third reading.
